title: The Only Dense Reward That Is Free

body:
In October 2024 a paper on reinforcement learning for LLM reasoning reported that adding a process reward model on top of a verifiable outcome reward made training collapse, and that two patches rescued it. The second, which the authors call Delta, "drops the last-step reward and computes the difference of rewards between two adjacent steps." That is potential-based reward shaping. It was proved correct in 1999, it is the only form of dense per-step reward that provably leaves the optimal policy alone, and the field rediscovered it empirically a quarter-century later while trying to stop a model padding its chain of thought.

The theorem is stranger than "differencing is a good idea." It says the space of dense rewards splits cleanly in two; that one half costs nothing and the other half changes what you are optimizing; and — the part that should sting — that a dense reward from the second half is not a hint. It is a different objective, adopted silently.

## The sparse-reward era made everyone reach for density

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards gives one bit per rollout: thousands of tokens generated, a single scalar back, attached to the last one. Every instinct in RL says to densify that, and process reward models are how the field does it — a model scoring intermediate steps, usually as $p(\text{step is correct})$ or $p(\text{eventual success} \mid \text{prefix})$, whose scores are added to the outcome reward at each step.

Both quantities are *levels*. The first is a property of a step, the second very nearly a value function. Neither is a difference, and adding a level at every step is exactly the operation the 1999 theorem identifies as unsafe. Worse, LLM RL almost always runs at $\gamma = 1$, removing the one thing that bounded the damage in classical RL.

## Policy invariance, in one substitution

Take an MDP $M = (S, A, P, \gamma, R)$ and a shaped $M' = (S, A, P, \gamma, R + F)$, where $F(s,a,s')$ is extra reward on the transition $s \to s'$. Ng, Harada and Russell call $F$ *potential-based* if there is some $\Phi : S \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$F(s,a,s') ;=; \gamma,\Phi(s') - \Phi(s).$$

Sufficiency is guess-and-verify on the Bellman optimality equation. Propose $Q^{*}_{M'} = Q^{*}_{M} - \Phi$ and substitute:

$$\mathbb{E}\Big[R + \gamma\Phi(s') - \Phi(s) + \gamma \max_{a'} \big(Q^{*}{M}(s',a') - \Phi(s')\big)\Big] = \mathbb{E}\Big[R + \gamma \max{a'} Q^{*}_{M}(s',a')\Big] - \Phi(s),$$

because the $+\gamma\Phi(s')$ from the shaping and the $-\gamma\Phi(s')$ from the recursion cancel exactly. The right-hand side is $Q^{*}_{M}(s,a) - \Phi(s)$, so the proposal satisfies the fixed point. The shaped optimal action-value is the original shifted by a quantity independent of $a$, so the argmax is untouched: the optimal policies of $M'$ and $M$ coincide.

Two features of that proof matter more than the result. First, nothing was assumed about $\Phi$: it need not resemble the value function, be accurate, or be monotone in progress, and a wildly wrong $\Phi$ still preserves the optimum. You cannot corrupt the objective with a bad potential, only the optimization. Second, the whole thing was a change of variables on $Q$, which is why Wiewiora could show in 2003 that potential-based shaping and $Q$-value initialization are *equivalent* — an agent initialized at $-\Phi$ makes the same updates as one receiving the shaping rewards, and under a broad class of policies the two are behaviourally indistinguishable. Whatever a potential-based process reward is worth, it is worth an initialization.

The same authors proved the converse: if $F$ is not potential-based then, absent further knowledge of $P$ and $R$, one can construct dynamics and rewards consistent with $F$ under which the optimal policies of $M'$ are suboptimal in $M$. A worst case, but not exotic. Randløv and Alstrøm had just built an agent that learned to ride a bicycle and gave it positive reward for transitions toward the goal; it found that riding in circles of 20–50 metres collected that reward forever and never went anywhere.

## Why the tree has the same disease as the cycle

The token-level MDP has no cycles. Its state is the prefix $x_{<t}$, prefixes only grow, and the transition graph is a tree, so the bicycle's failure mode — a closed loop with positive net reward — is structurally impossible. Why does dense-reward hacking happen anyway?

Because a cycle was never the requirement; unbounded *length* suffices. Apply a level scorer $v: S \to \mathbb{R}$ at every step and the return is

$$J(\tau) ;=; R_{\text{outcome}}(\tau) + \sum_{t=0}^{T-1} \gamma^{t}, v(x_{t+1}),$$

which at $\gamma = 1$ is $\Theta(T)$ for any $v$ bounded away from zero. The model is paid per step for looking good, and the cheapest way to look good more often is to emit more steps. Run the same $v$ through the potential form and the sum collapses:

$$\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\big(v(x_{t+1}) - v(x_t)\big) ;=; v(x_T) - v(x_0),$$

independent of $T$. Differencing converts a length-proportional bonus into a length-invariant one. This is my reading rather than a claim any of these papers makes, but it accounts for the hack Gao and colleagues observed — the model "repeating correct but unnecessary reasoning steps" — better than the usual misspecification story, because it would happen with a *perfectly calibrated* PRM. Calibration is irrelevant when the pathology lives in the summation.

A second detail almost everyone gets wrong: the telescoping is exact only if you pay the tail. Over a trajectory terminating at $T$,

$$\sum_{t=0}^{T-1} \gamma^{t}\big(\gamma\Phi(x_{t+1}) - \Phi(x_t)\big) ;=; \gamma^{T}\Phi(x_T) - \Phi(x_0).$$

The $\Phi(x_0)$ term is a per-prompt constant and harmless. The $\gamma^T \Phi(x_T)$ term is not. In the textbook treatment the terminal state is absorbing and you eventually pay back $-\Phi$ forever; real implementations truncate and never pay it. Unless $\Phi$ vanishes at terminal states you have added a length-dependent term: at $\gamma < 1$ with positive terminal potential, shorter is strictly better; at $\gamma = 1$ you counted the final step twice. PRMs score highest exactly at the terminal step, so this is not a corner case. Zero your potential at termination.

## The right object was the difference all along

Nothing asks $\Phi$ to be good, but one choice is distinguished. Set $\Phi = V^{*}$:

$$\mathbb{E}\big[R(s,a,s') + \gamma V^{*}(s') - V^{*}(s)\big] ;=; Q^{*}(s,a) - V^{*}(s) ;=; A^{*}(s,a) \le 0.$$

The shaped reward *is* the advantage: zero along optimal actions, negative in proportion to what a step costs you. A correct step earns nothing — the exact opposite of what a PRM is trained to emit. A PRM predicts something close to $V$, a level, and that level is used as the reward. The object you wanted was its difference.

Setlur and colleagues reach the same place from another direction. Their process advantage verifiers score a step by *progress* — an advantage under a separate prover policy — rather than by absolute correctness under the base policy, reporting better than 8% accuracy over outcome reward models, 1.5–5× compute efficiency, and 5–6× sample efficiency for online RL. Since $\Phi = V^{\text{prover}}$ is the value of a policy other than the one being trained, PAV is not literally PBRS. The theorem says why that is fine: *any* $\Phi$ preserves the optimum, so the prover is a free choice made to speed up learning.

Does this survive the KL term? RLHF maximizes $\mathbb{E}[\sum_t r] - \beta,\mathrm{KL}(\pi ,|, \pi_{\text{ref}})$, not raw return. It does, for the same one-line reason: the regularized optimal policy is $\pi^{*}(a\mid s) \propto \pi_{\text{ref}}(a \mid s)\exp!\big(Q_{\text{soft}}(s,a)/\beta\big)$, and a state-only potential shifts $Q_{\text{soft}}$ by $-\Phi(s)$, constant in $a$ and absorbed by the normalizer. Rafailov and colleagues observe the dual fact: in the token-level MDP under the max-entropy formulation, the log-ratio $\beta \log \pi/\pi_{\text{ref}}$ acts as an implicit token-level reward or advantage, invariant under shaping. DPO's per-token credit assignment is a potential difference by construction — the cleanest explanation of why DPO never needed a PRM to be dense.

## Three states, and the arithmetic

Let $S = {s_0, s_1, s_2}$ with $s_2$ terminal, one unit of reward for reaching it, $\gamma = 0.9$, and a PRM-like progress score $v(s_0) = 0$, $v(s_1) = 0.5$, $v(s_2) = 1$. The unshaped value of finishing is $0.9$. Add $v$ as a level — standard practice — so each transition pays $v(s')$:

- Finish, $s_0 \to s_1 \to s_2$: $0.5 + 0.9(1 + 1) = 2.30$.
- Oscillate forever between $s_0$ and $s_1$: $0.5(1 + \gamma^2 + \gamma^4 + \cdots) = 0.5 / 0.19 = 2.63$.

Stalling beats solving by 14%, with a sensible progress score and no misspecification anywhere. Now the potential form with $\Phi = v$ and $\Phi(s_2) = 0$: finishing gives $0.9 + (\gamma^2 \cdot 0 - 0) = 0.9$, exactly the unshaped value, and oscillating gives $0$. The ordering is restored and the shaped values equal the true ones. Leave $\Phi(s_2) = 1$ and truncate instead, and finishing in two steps scores $0.9 + \gamma^2 = 1.71$ against $1.54$ for three — the length bias, on schedule.

The fix costs one line and applies to any per-step scorer you have:

```python
import numpy as np
def potentialize(v, gamma=1.0, zero_terminal=True):
    """v: PRM levels v(x_0) .. v(x_T). Returns T shaping rewards."""
    v = np.asarray(v, dtype=float).copy()
    if zero_terminal:
        v[-1] = 0.0
    return gamma * v[1:] - v[:-1]
def length_bias(seqs, gamma=1.0, potential=False):
    """Corr(episode length, total shaping return). Potential-based => ~0."""
    tot, lens = [], []
    for v in seqs:
        F = potentialize(v, gamma) if potential else np.asarray(v[1:], float)
        tot.append(float(F @ gamma ** np.arange(len(F))))
        lens.append(len(F))
    return float(np.corrcoef(lens, tot)[0, 1])
Run `length_bias` on a batch of rollouts before you run RL on them. A strongly positive correlation means your dense reward is paying for tokens, and no PRM quality fixes that.
```

## What to do on Monday

Never add a level; difference it. This is free, needs no retraining, and is the highest-value change available to anyone summing PRM scores into a reward. Zero the potential at termination while you are there.

Then ask the harder question: if you already run PPO with a critic, what is the PRM for? Under $\Phi = V^{\pi}$ the shaped reward is the advantage, which GAE already estimates from the critic. A PRM earns its place only if it is a *better* value estimator — plausible when the critic is small and undertrained and the PRM saw far more data, much less plausible otherwise. What you are buying is an initialization, not a goal.

Two edge cases. If the scorer depends on the action, differencing is insufficient and you want Wiewiora, Cottrell and Elkan's look-ahead advice. If the potential changes during training — as in PRIME — Devlin and Kudenko cover time-varying $\Phi_t$, but a replay buffer holding shaping computed under a since-updated $\Phi$ is outside their guarantee.

And if you actually want to change the optimum — shorter proofs, legible steps, no unsafe partial reasoning — say so. Write it as a stated objective term rather than smuggling it in as "shaping," and the theorem will tell you what you gave up.

## Where this argument is weaker than it sounds

Policy invariance concerns the *optimal* policy, and nobody reaches it. Under a fixed compute budget with a function approximator and an early stop, what you ship sits somewhere along a trajectory, and shaping changes that trajectory — the entire point of using it. Invariance of a limit you never attain is weaker than it sounds. Necessity is weak in the other direction: worst-case over MDPs consistent with $F$, silent on whether yours is a bad one.

Differencing also changes the reward's *scale*. If the PRM's level is $O(1)$ and moves smoothly, its differences are $O(1/T)$, so against a fixed $\beta$ the dense signal is far quieter. Gao and colleagues' Delta result is confounded twice over: with Clip, applied alongside it, and with the fact that making a signal potential-based also shrinks it. Nobody has run the ablation separating those. The rest of the evidence is thinner still — SHAPE (ACL 2026) reports 3% accuracy with 30% fewer tokens, but changes segment advantages and adds entropy-driven token redistribution at once, so its token reduction is what a length-invariant return predicts rather than proof of one.

There is a supply problem underneath all of this. The Qwen team found that Monte-Carlo-estimated process labels — the cheap way to build a PRM — generalize worse than LLM-as-judge or human annotation, since a completion model's success rate from a prefix conflates step correctness with recoverability. If $\Phi$ is that noisy, potential-basedness protects the objective perfectly and does nothing for variance, which was the only thing shaping was for.

The deepest objection is that invariance may be the wrong thing to want. Lightman and colleagues' case for process supervision was partly that rewarding a chain of reasoning a human endorses is safer than rewarding an answer, especially when the answer-checker is gameable. That is an argument for a process reward that *does* move the optimum, and a good one. But it is incompatible with the far more common claim that the process reward merely helps the model find the same optimum faster, and the two get asserted in the same breath more often than either is defended. You can have policy invariance, or a process reward that changes what the model is for. The 1999 theorem's service is not telling you which to pick. It is making the bill impossible to hide.

## Further reading

*A note on retrieval: arXiv, ACL Anthology, OpenReview, PMLR and every other paper repository were blocked by this session's egress policy, so the sources below were located through search rather than by fetching full texts. Titles, venues and URLs are as retrieved; figures are as stated in retrieved abstracts. The length-invariance argument, terminal-potential derivation and three-state arithmetic are mine.*

- Ng, Harada, Russell, *Policy Invariance Under Reward Transformations*, ICML 1999, 278–287. [dl.acm.org](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.5555/645528.657613) — the theorem, both directions.
- Randløv, Alstrøm, *Learning to Drive a Bicycle Using Reinforcement Learning and Shaping*, ICML 1998. [gwern.net](https://gwern.net/doc/reinforcement-learning/model-free/1998-randlov.pdf) — the failure that motivated it; read it for how reasonable the shaping looked.
- Wiewiora, *Potential-Based Shaping and Q-Value Initialization are Equivalent*, JAIR 19:205–208, 2003. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1106.5267) — four pages that price shaping exactly.
- Wiewiora, Cottrell, Elkan, *Principled Methods for Advising Reinforcement Learning Agents*, ICML 2003. [dl.acm.org](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.5555/3041838.3041938) — look-ahead advice, for when the scorer sees the action.
- *Expressing Arbitrary Reward Functions as Potential-Based Advice*, AAAI 2015. [cdn.aaai.org](https://cdn.aaai.org/ojs/9628/9628-13-13156-1-2-20201228.pdf) — converting an arbitrary reward rather than discarding it.
- Devlin, Kudenko, *Dynamic Potential-Based Reward Shaping*, AAMAS 2012, 433–440. [eprints.whiterose.ac.uk](https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/75121/2/p433_devlin.pdf) — time-varying potentials; what online-updated process models need.
- Lightman et al., *Let's Verify Step by Step*, arXiv:2305.20050. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.20050) — made process supervision standard; also PRM800K.
- Setlur et al., *Rewarding Progress: Scaling Automated Process Verifiers for LLM Reasoning*, arXiv:2410.08146, ICLR 2025. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.08146) — progress under a prover policy instead of correctness under the base policy. The most important recent paper here.
- Gao et al., *On Designing Effective RL Reward at Training Time for LLM Reasoning*, arXiv:2410.15115. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.15115) — collapse from PRM-as-shaping, and the Clip and Delta fixes. The rediscovery this post is about.
- Cui et al., *Process Reinforcement through Implicit Rewards*, arXiv:2502.01456. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.01456) — token rewards as a log-probability ratio; a dynamic potential in all but name.
- *The Lessons of Developing Process Reward Models in Mathematical Reasoning*, arXiv:2501.07301, Findings of ACL 2025. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.07301) — why Monte-Carlo process labels are worse than they look.
- Rafailov, Hejna, Park, Finn, *From r to Q*: Your Language Model is Secretly a Q-Function*, COLM 2024, arXiv:2404.12358. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.12358) — DPO's implicit token reward, invariant under shaping.
- *SHAPE: Stage-aware Hierarchical Advantage via Potential Estimation for LLM Reasoning*, arXiv:2604.06636, ACL 2026. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.06636) — the newest attempt to build the potential explicitly; read the ablations sceptically.
